sections.text:
Romans 8 is a high point of Paul’s letter. It opens with “no condemnation” for those who are in Christ Jesus and closes with the assurance that nothing can separate them from God’s love.

In between, Paul contrasts two ways of living: according to the flesh, meaning human nature turned away from God, and according to the Spirit. Those led by the Spirit are God’s children and can call him “Abba! Father!”

Paul is honest about suffering. The whole creation “groans”, believers groan while they wait, and the Spirit helps in prayer when words fail. Verse 28 belongs with verses 29 and 30: the good that God works toward is that his people become like his Son.

Paul wrote this letter to Christians in Rome, a church he had not yet visited, probably in the mid to late 50s of the first century. The church included both Jewish and non-Jewish believers, and much of the letter deals with how God makes both right with himself.

“Abba” is an Aramaic word for father, from the language Jesus spoke. Mark 14:36 records Jesus using it in prayer. Adoption was familiar in the Roman world: an adopted son received the family name and the full rights of an heir, which is the picture behind verses 15 to 17.

Verses 29 and 30 are read differently across traditions.

- Reformed Christians understand “foreknew” and “predestined” as God’s free choice of those he will save.
- Arminian and Wesleyan Christians understand that God foreknew who would believe, and predestined those believers to become like Christ.
- Others stress that Paul is speaking about God’s people as a whole and about where God is taking them.

All agree on the purpose Paul names: being “conformed to the image of his Son”. Verse 28 is sometimes quoted on its own as a promise that everything will turn out pleasant. In its setting it is spoken to people who suffer, and the good in view is that likeness to Christ.

translations.note: WEB and the KJV continue with “who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit”; the ASV ends the verse at Christ Jesus. The longer wording is missing from the oldest manuscripts at this point. The same words stand in verse 4 in all of them.

renderings.text: who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit
There is therefore now no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus.

translations.note: The Greek word for Spirit is grammatically neuter, and the KJV follows the grammar. The ASV and WEB say “himself”, because the passage speaks of the Spirit as one who testifies and prays.

renderings.text: The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit
